newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTORCYCLING-DOOHAN SET TO CATCH "MIKE THE BIKE".
newsitem.headline: MOTORCYCLING-DOOHAN SET TO CATCH "MIKE THE BIKE".

text.p: Sunday's Italian Grand Prix at Mugello in the rolling hills of Tuscany could see 500cc world champion Michael Doohan pull level with the late Mike "The Bike" Hailwood in motorcycling's list of winners.
The slender 31-year-old Australian, winner of three consecutive world titles, needs one more victory to level with the Briton's tally of 37 career 500cc wins.
Not that Doohan is the sort of man to be obsessed by statistics. Or that the figure means that much, given that the great Italian Giacamo Agostino won 68 Grands Prix.
"History doesn't do much for the world championship or winning races," he said last year when his victory at Mugello made him the highest points scorer in 500cc history.
That was another misleading figure since a win now is worth 25 points compared to the 10 in days of old.
However, a fifth win in five years at Mugello would give the Australian the concrete satisfaction of stretching his lead at the top of the standings from Honda team mate Alex Criville.
Criville pipped Doohan into second place in the last race in his native Spain and has 65 points to Doohan's 70.
Doohan won the first two races of the season and is the clear favourite to lead the field again on Sunday. Criville was second in the opening two races.
No European has won the 500 world title since Italian Franco Uncini on a Suzuki in 1982 and Criville looks the best prospect in a sport long dominated by Americans and Australians.

Despite their being team mates, there seems to be little love lost between the two men who have few genuine rivals in a season that has already thrown up one inescapable conclusion -- if you don't ride a Honda you don't have much chance.
Three Hondas filled the top three places in the season-opener in Malaysia, six took the top six in Japan and five swept the top five at Jerez earlier this month.
The top six in the world standings are all Honda riders.

"The 500s have become a Honda trophy and that certainly isn't good for the sport," Doohan was quoted as saying at Jerez, reportedly criticising his employers for making too many four-cylinder NSR 500s available.
Italy's 500c hopes rest primarily with Luca Cadalora on a Yamaha and Doriano Romboni on the V-twin Italian Aprilia.
Romboni finished sixth in Jerez, returning from a nine-month injury layoff and starting in 19th place on the grid.
Cadalora has a new sponsor but not much more hope on an out of sorts bike that cannot match the Hondas on the straights. "It'll be a tough race," he said recently.
As far as most of the local fans are concerned, the 500cc race might as well not be run.

Some may be excused for not even knowing that it is happening since the big stars in Italy are in the 250cc and 125cc classes with three times world 250 champion Max Biaggi the big draw with teenage 125 rider Valentino Rossi.
Race reports in the Italian newspapers after Jerez barely mentioned the outcome of the 500cc race.
